newsitem.title: UK: BA flights hit, says no strikers suspended.
newsitem.headline: BA flights hit, says no strikers suspended.

text.p: British Airways said on Monday normal service on its worldwide network would not resume until later in the week but denied it had suspended cabin crew who went on strike last week.

BA expects to talk with leaders of the 9,000 cabin crew later this week to try and resolve their dispute over pay. It still faces a possible walkout by caterers, baggage handlers and check-in staff in a separate spat.
"We're hoping to restore a full programme (of flights) by mid-week," a BA spokeswoman told Reuters.
She said flight problems were exacerbated by the fact that out of 2,000 cabin crew who called in sick last week only 200 had so far reported in for work.

"There are still significant numbers of aircraft and crew out of position, it's going to take us a little while to get the operation back to normal, but we're trying our best to do it as soon as possible," she said.
BA's schedules were thrown into disarray and thousands of passengers were stranded last week during the 72-hour cabin crew strike over pay and conditions.
The bill for the walkout already runs into tens of millions of pounds, analysts estimate, and has further soured relations between BA management and employees.
Cabin crew unions object to the imposition of a company plan to save 42 million pounds ($71 million) as part of its strategy to improve competitiveness.

In the separate dispute over the planned sell-off of the airline's catering unit at Heathrow airport, BA's caterers will meet at 1130 GMT to decide whether to hold further talks or to take industrial action.
The 1,400 workers, members of the Transport and General Workers' Union (T&G), have rejected company proposals aimed at protecting their terms and conditions after the sale.

Cabin crew leaders will this week send BA's chief executive Bob Ayling written proposals on how the union can help the company make the savings, a spokesman for the T&G, the main union involved in the dispute, said.
"There is no question of further strikes until BA has considered our proposals. There has been a more positive move towards talks," Andrew Murray of the T&G said.

However, the T&G said there would be no talks if they found evidence that cabin crew members had been suspended or were being victimised by being left off the roster and therefore not being paid as a result of striking.
"We've got a meeting at three o'clock (1400 GMT), if this victimisation issue hasn't been cleared up by then, then the 'pause for peace' could be over," he said.
BA denied that any cabin crew employee was being punished, but noted that some would have to wait to be rostered while airline operations got back to normal.

"No one is being suspended. Staff will be paid as soon as they are rostered to work, within a few days at the most," the BA spokeswoman said. "Airline rostering is a complex affair and requires a degree of planning."
She said BA would not sue or dismiss strikers as it had threatened last week -- but they still risked losing travel perks, promotion and severance opportunities.
The airline also said stewards and stewardesses were being asked for an assurance that they were now prepared to work normally.
BA expects 74 out of its 122 European flights from London Heathrow airport to operate on Monday, while 41 out of 48 daily long-haul flights and 32 out of 60 domestic services will run.
Out of London Gatwick, all long-haul flights bar one are operating today while both European and UK domestic services retain a full quota.
($ = 0.591 British Pounds)
